Title: A huge load off my shoulders
NewsSummary: International student Job Otieno describes how financial aid helped him pursue his dream.
NewsContent:
"Money was the single biggest worry in my life," recalls Job Otieno, 25, an international student pursuing the Associate of Science in Dental Hygiene, ASDH, degree at AKU's Karachi campus. 

Like most Kenyans, Job was expected to move out and live independently after completing college in 2018. Youth unemployment is a major issue in Kenya and Job initially had to take up a number of casual jobs in hospitality and customer service to make ends meet. 

"I used to feel stuck because financial issues always got in the way of my ambition to study. I could only do what was important at the moment and could never plan for the future," he remembers.

In 2019, after a year of hustling to support himself, Job's life took a turn for the better when he started work as a housekeeper at the Aga Khan University Hospital's dental clinic in Nairobi. Even though life was still hard with rent and commuting costs covering the majority of his salary, his job exposed him to an environment that provided regular inspiration. 

"People would come to the clinic in pain, but they would leave with big smiles," remembers Job. Being around people who were striving to help others appealed to him, and Job was seriously considering higher studies in dental hygiene until a familiar challenge returned to halt his plans. 

"The cost of the application fee was half of my salary and I just didn't have the money," Job recalls. 

Fortunately, the clinic's manager, Shaida Pirani, who recognised his potential and continues to be a constant source of support for Job, came to his aid at the time by paying the fee. While this enabled him to apply for the ASDH programme, there were still obstacles to overcome.

"I was counting up the cost of everything down to the shilling: the degree, the flight, applying for a passport, the visa and it just wasn't adding up." 

After speaking to ASDH alumni, faculty and the programme's directors, Job decided to apply for financial aid. The coming months saw him face a number of delays in obtaining his visa and a host of challenges in receiving his first passport. But the struggle proved to be worth it when he received an email confirming that he had received 75 per cent financial assistance to study at AKU. 

"I used to feel like I was carrying a huge load on a long, uncertain journey. Then someone came along, took off the load and just dropped me off at my destination. That's what financial aid did for me, it left me completely humbled and renewed my optimism about the future."

Job has now completed the first year of his two-year programme and he is already making plans about how to apply his knowledge. Learning about the connections between the environment and oral health (systemic health) during his degree has inspired him to advocate for essential reforms to the water and sanitation infrastructure.  

"Many people in Kenya suffer from oral health issues because they lack access to clean water," Job says. "It's a major issue in my country and I want to change this narrative upon my return."
